title: Neighborhood Walk Scavenger Hunt, Free Printable List
metaDescription: Turn a walk around the block into a game with this free printable neighborhood scavenger hunt. 28 sidewalk, street and porch spots, print in Letter or A4.
intro: Print a free neighborhood walk scavenger hunt with 28 things to spot on a stroll around the block. It turns an ordinary evening walk into a game.
items: A house number with a 7 in it
A garden gnome or lawn ornament | 2
A tree with blossoms or colored leaves
A chalk drawing on the sidewalk | 3
A bicycle locked up or leaning on a fence
A street name beginning with your first initial | 2
A book-sharing box on a post | 3
A pair of stairs with more than ten steps
A house with a porch swing
Something that starts with the letter B
A tree you could climb if you were allowed. Look only
itemsNote: All 28 items are ready in the generator above. Walk your own route first, then cut what is not there and add a landmark every child on your street would know.

sections.heading: How to turn a stroll into a hunt
body: The idea is to look at a familiar street with new eyes. Children who have passed the same corner a hundred times suddenly notice the wind vane, the painted door and the stairs.

1. Walk the route yourself or study it on a map, and decide where the loop starts and ends.
2. Print a sheet per child. Pairs of siblings can share a sheet and take turns holding the pencil.
3. Explain the rules before you leave: stay on the sidewalk, cross only with an adult and never go up to a house.
4. Ask children to call out sightings rather than racing ahead. A shared list means everybody ticks the same thing at the same moment.
5. Back at home, count the boxes ticked and talk about the most surprising find.

sections.heading: Ways to play it differently
body:
* **Letter walk.** Pick a letter of the alphabet and have children find a sign, house or object starting with it. The sheet works as a warm-up, and the letter game takes over from there.
* **Seasonal swap.** Replace a few items with things that suit the time of year, like pumpkins in October or string lights in December.
* **Grown-ups versus kids.** Adults and children each get a copy and see who finishes first. It makes a long walk with a reluctant walker much shorter.

sections.heading: Tips for families and groups
body: Neighborhood hunts work well as a regular habit. A Sunday walk with a fresh list keeps children interested in their own surroundings, and you can use the shuffle option to give everyone a different starting item.

Be mindful of privacy. Items are meant to be spotted from the public sidewalk, not photographed through windows. If your children use a camera, ask them to leave people and private spaces out of the picture.

sections.heading: Road and street safety
body: Stay on sidewalks, hold hands near busy roads and cross only at crossings with a grown-up. Keep children close, especially at dusk, and choose a route you know. Do not enter driveways or yards, and teach children not to approach strangers or dogs they do not know.

sections.heading: Printing for a walk
body: Print one page per child and fold it in half to fit in a back pocket. A rolled elastic band around the pencil and paper stops either from getting lost. The tool works in black and white and uses very little ink in checklist layout, which helps if you print a new route list each weekend.

faq.q: What is a good length for a neighborhood scavenger hunt?
faq.a: A loop of about 15 to 30 minutes suits young children. For older children, a longer walk with all 28 items can fill an hour.

faq.q: Do we have to walk the whole route to finish?
faq.a: No. The list is built so most of it can be found on a short loop. Skip anything that is not in your area and add local favorites such as a corner bakery or a big old tree.

faq.q: Is this suitable for a block party?
faq.a: It is. Print one copy per child, give out stickers as prizes and let neighbors help by pointing out the harder finds.
